The American purple gallinule (Porphyrio martinica) exhibits a complex life history that begins with eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature regime that supports an incubation period of approximately 23.5 days [ab = approximately 23.5 days]. This duration, which aligns with the typical range of 22 to 25 days reported for rallid species, reflects the thermoregulatory demands placed on incubating adults as they maintain stable nest temperatures amid fluctuating wetland microclimates. Upon hatching, precocial chicks emerge weighing roughly 13.4 grams [Wwb = roughly 13.4 grams], a modest neonatal mass that underscores the considerable energetic investment the species makes in producing a relatively small number of well-developed offspring. The chicks are soon capable of moving through floating vegetation, though they remain dependent on parental brooding and feeding for several weeks. The initial wet weight of newly hatched individuals, measured shortly after emergence and before any feeding, stands at 18 grams [Ww0 = 18 grams], indicating that a small amount of residual yolk mass is still present immediately after the hatching process is complete.

Under typical thermal conditions experienced by active juveniles in their subtropical and tropical range, which generally hover around 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] during the warm season, sexual maturation occurs at 189 days after hatching [tp = 189 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid progression to puberty is characteristic of many rallid species inhabiting productive wetlands where food resources are abundant year-round, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition to support the onset of gonadal development. In contrast, the first successful breeding attempt is generally deferred until an individual is 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the need to acquire a breeding territory and establish a pair bond within the dense marsh vegetation at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This timing means that most individuals do not contribute to the next generation until their second calendar year of life, even though they are physiologically capable of reproduction much earlier. The interval between achieving sexual maturity and initiating a first brood represents a period of social and ecological fine-tuning that may influence overall lifetime reproductive success.

Adult body mass in this species shows pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a pattern not uncommon among rails. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 215 grams [Wwi = approximately 215 grams], whereas adult males are substantially heavier, reaching a maximum body mass of 257 grams [Wwi = 257 grams]. This difference of over 40 grams likely has implications for both foraging ecology and competitive interactions, as the larger males may dominate access to preferred feeding areas within the floating vegetation mats that characterize their habitat. The mass data were compiled from multiple field studies across the species' range, from the southeastern United States through Central America and into South America, and reflect measurements taken from breeding adults captured during the peak of the nesting season. Such values are consistent with those reported for other medium-bodied members of the genus Porphyrio, though the American species tends toward the smaller end of the spectrum compared to its larger Old World congeners.

Fledging marks a critical developmental milestone in the life cycle of the American purple gallinule. Under thermal conditions typical of the active growing season around 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], young birds achieve first sustained flight at 63 days after hatching [tx = 63 days after hatching]. This is notably longer than the initial period of brood dependency, which lasts from approximately 21 to 25 days, after which the chicks begin to forage independently but remain within the family group. The extended pre-fledging interval allows the development of the strong flight muscles and fully functional wings necessary for maneuvering through the cluttered marsh environment, as well as for evading predators such as herons and large wading birds. Field observations indicate that during this protracted nestling period, both parents contribute equally to provisioning, delivering a variety of aquatic invertebrates and plant material to the developing young. The fledgling stage is followed by a period of post-fledging parental care that may last several additional weeks before the young birds disperse.

Field studies have recorded a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years] for free-living individuals under typical thermal regimes around 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This lifespan, while modest by the standards of some long-lived waterbirds, is sufficient to support a reproductive strategy centered on a single annual breeding attempt. Females typically lay between 5 and 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 5 and 10 eggs per clutch], with approximately 6.5 clutches produced each year [F_R_i = approximately 6.5 clutches produced each year]. The combination of a moderate clutch size and multiple nesting attempts annually means that annual reproductive output is potentially high, placing a premium on high hatching and fledging success rates within each brood. This life-history pattern is well-suited to stable wetland environments where nest predation and flooding risks are predictable, but it may limit the species' ability to recover rapidly from population declines caused by habitat loss or severe weather events.
